title: Reachability is a design material
summary: A benefit can be real on paper and unreachable in practice. Interfaces should expose the distance between eligibility and actual help.
body: Directories usually answer a database question: does a program exist? A person in need is asking something harder: can I reach it, am I safe applying, how long will it take, and what happens next?

That gap changes the product. Rank by practical reachability. Put status-safety and time-to-help near the top. Link every consequential claim to a source. Make uncertainty visible instead of laundering it through a clean interface.

title: Nostalgia is an instrument, not a costume
summary: Old interfaces and physical tools matter when their constraints change the work—not when they merely signal taste.
body: A CRT, a sequencer, or a terminal typeface can become empty shorthand. The useful question is what the older tool makes possible: a slower decision, a tactile route, a limitation that forces a point of view.

This site borrows the logic of a studio rather than someone else's room. Every object has a narrative job, every visual route has a direct semantic equivalent, and the atmosphere never gets to hide the work.

title: Name the proof state
summary: A prototype, deployment, launch, purchase, and outcome are five different claims. Good product storytelling says which one is true.
body: Polish makes it easy to overstate what happened. A working interface can prove the interaction. A public URL can prove deployment. Neither proves adoption or impact.
Treat evidence like a design system: define the states, label them consistently, and leave the unknowns visible. Trust compounds when the portfolio tells the difference.
